Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Boston Logan International Airport, Boston MA - Facility Tour
Tour-Category: facility

Stop 1: Terminal A

Address: 1 Harborside Dr, Boston, MA 02128

Coordinates: 42.3704, -71.0202

Type/Specialty: Airport Terminal

Specific Examples: Check-in counters, security checkpoints, dining options

Operational Details: Open 24/7, varies by airline for check-in times, typically busy during morning and evening rush hours

Orientation: You are about to embark on a walking journey through Boston Logan International Airport, Boston MA. From Terminal A to the terminal entrance vestibule, you'll traverse the interconnected spaces where human movement converges. The air traffic control tower cabin stands as a testament to the historical evolution of aviation infrastructure. Witness firsthand how meticulous planning and technological advancements have shaped the seamless orchestration of air travel within these walls. Your first stop is Terminal A. From the Airport T station, take the elevator up to the terminal level and follow the signs to Terminal A. You will notice the modern architecture as you approach the terminal. As you approach Terminal A at Boston Logan International Airport, the hum of departing flights fills the air. This bustling hub, known for its sleek design and eco-friendly features, exemplifies modern airport innovation.

Reconstructed and reopened in 2005, it became the world’s first airport terminal to receive LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) certification. This accolade, awarded by the U.S. Green Building Council, recognizes the terminal's commitment to sustainable architecture, including energy efficiency and reduced carbon footprint. The history of Terminal A is deeply intertwined with the airport's evolution. Originally, this site housed the Eastern Airlines shuttle hub, designed in the late 1960s by Yamasaki & Associates, the same firm that crafted the iconic World Trade Center towers. Although that terminal was eventually demolished, its legacy of architectural excellence lives on through the new Terminal A. Boston Logan International Airport, named after Major General Edward Lawrence Logan, occupies a significant place in both local and aviation history. In 1943, the Massachusetts state legislature chose to honor General Logan, a South Boston native and World War I commander of the 101st Infantry Regiment, by renaming the airport after him. His contributions as a municipal judge and state legislator further cemented his status as a prominent figure in Massachusetts' history. Terminal A's reconstruction marked a turning point: it addressed post-9/11 security needs, making it a model for integrating safety into airport design. This transformation involved not only architectural innovation but also a strategic focus on passenger safety and efficiency. Today, Boston Logan International Airport sprawls over 2,384 acres and serves as a major hub with six runways and four passenger terminals. In 2024, the airport achieved a record by handling 43.5 million passengers, underscoring its role as a crucial gateway for domestic and international travel. The vibrant atmosphere at Terminal A is a reminder of the complex coordination and infrastructure that underpin modern air travel, ensuring that each flight departs smoothly and safely.


Directions: From Terminal A, head towards the central terminal area. Once there, continue walking towards the direction of the boarding gate desks. Look for signs directing you to your specific gate, and you'll reach the boarding gate desk in no time.



Stop 2: boarding gate desk

Address: 1 Harborside Dr, Boston, MA 02128

Coordinates: 42.3662, -71.0205

Type/Specialty: Gate Area

Specific Examples: Boarding announcements, seating areas, display screens

Operational Details: Operational hours vary by flight schedule, no fees, seating is first-come, first-served

Orientation: Position yourself to best view this location.

Here, the boarding gate desk serves as more than just a transition point; it is a place deeply embedded in history. On September 11, 2001, hijackers boarded Flights 11 and 175 here, setting off events that reshaped global security and air travel protocols. This unassuming locale also witnessed the signing of Chapter 404 of the Acts of 1922, when Massachusetts Governor Channing H. Cox authorized leasing state-owned tidal flats in East Boston to construct an airfield, laying the groundwork for what would become this bustling airport. The gate agents today are unsung heroes, managing last-minute changes that ripple through the airport, yet their decisions swiftly travel across terminals like the one you explored at Terminal A earlier. Looking forward, how these changes are communicated illustrates the real-time orchestration essential to modern air travel.


Directions: Alright, from the boarding gate desk, head towards Terminal C. Walk past the TSA security checkpoint and continue on foot through the terminal. Once you exit the terminal, stroll towards the air traffic control tower cabin located near the airport's control tower.



Stop 3: air traffic control tower cabin

Address: 1 Harborside Dr, Boston, MA 02128

Coordinates: 42.3660, -71.0205

Type/Specialty: Control Tower

Specific Examples: Views of aircraft takeoffs and landings, radar screens, control room operations

Operational Details: Access is restricted, tours by appointment only, typically busy during peak flight hours

Orientation: As you stand here in the air traffic control tower cabin at Boston Logan International Airport, take a moment to look out over the bustling runways. The view from this vantage point is a testament to the airport's extensive operations, guiding more than 1,200 flights daily.

This air traffic control tower, designed Dean, Stahl & Rogers, stands as a remarkable feat of engineering and architecture. Completed in 1973, its twin cylindrical concrete pylons are an innovative departure from the single-shaft towers typically favored by the FAA at the time. This unique design is not just for aesthetic value; it speaks to the vision of Mayor James Michael Curley and aviation advocates who were determined to secure Boston's place on national airmail routes. Their efforts helped ensure that the airport remained a vital hub for both civilian and military aviation, including bases for the U.S. And the Massachusetts National Guard. The tower also connects to the airport's historical expansion efforts, which were managed by Massport, the authority overseeing transportation facilities, since 1959. Massport's approach to funding capital expansions through airport revenue bonds and federal grants, without relying on taxpayer money from the state's reflects a strategic and self-sustaining development philosophy. From this cabin, you can appreciate the complex orchestration required to manage such a high volume of traffic, ensuring that each flight transitions smoothly from ground to sky. With its distinctive design and historical significance, the tower is more than just a control center; it is a symbol of Boston's enduring commitment to aviation excellence.


Directions: As you leave the air traffic control tower cabin, walk towards Airport Road. Continue walking along Airport Road until you reach the terminal entrance vestibule. You'll pass by the airport hangars and parking lots on your way there. Just follow the flow of foot traffic towards the terminal entrance.



Stop 4: terminal entrance vestibule

Address: 1 Harborside Dr, Boston, MA 02128

Coordinates: 42.3662, -71.0200

Type/Specialty: Airport Entrance

Specific Examples: Baggage claim area, arrival signage, pick-up zones

Operational Details: Open 24/7, no fees for entry, can be busy during flight arrivals

Orientation: As you arrive at the Terminal Entrance Vestibule of Boston Logan International Airport, step slightly to the side to allow a full view of the bustling threshold. The flow of passengers here is a vivid reminder of the airport's role as a gateway to the world.

This stop places you at the juxtaposition of history and modernity. Once adjacent to the site of the 1969 Maverick Mothers protest—an event where determined local women stood their ground to protect their community from encroachment—this vestibule now symbolizes the resolve that has long characterized this area. Listen to the rhythmic ebb and flow of people, each traveler marking a brief yet significant chapter in the airport's bustling narrative. Established as Jeffery Field in 1923, Logan's historical roots trace back to its inception as a small airfield demanded by local civic leaders to ensure Boston's place in commercial commerce and airmail networks. Meanwhile, the station plays a role similar to Washington's Union Station, which burns brightly as a beacon of travel, powered since 1907 by Daniel Burnham's design. Both destinations serve as critical intermodal facilities linking cities across the U.S. and demonstrating an architectural evolution that marries utility with style.



That's 4 stops — Terminal A, site of the world's first LEED-certified airport terminal (2005 reopening) and Terminal entrance vestibule, symbolizing the Maverick Mothers protest site (1969 event). If you would like to eat nearby we can build you a restaurant tour.
